questions.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+4{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+7{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 
Calculate the norm of the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $‖v‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{3\cdot 3+4\cdot ((-2)\cdot (-2))+7\cdot (0\cdot 0)} \\  & =\sqrt{9+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V={R}_{2}[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(1)y(1)+x(0)y(0)+x(-1)y(-1).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $p(t)=2-3t+{t}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=2-3t+{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=0,\,p(0)=2,\,p(-1)=6.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(1)p(1)+p(0)p(0)+p(-1)p(-1)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(1)]^{2}+[p(0)]^{2}+[p(-1)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+4+36} \\  & =\sqrt{40} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[\pi ,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[\pi ,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =(\frac{2\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi }{4})-(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4}) \\  & =(\pi +0)-(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =3\cdot (2\cdot 2)+(-1)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot (1\cdot 1) \\  & =12+1+3 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{16}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
‖f(t)‖=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.

$$

questions.problem:
An inner product on $V={R}^{3}$ is defined as $⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3}.$ 

Normalize the  vector  $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product.
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot 2+3\cdot 1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+3+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $v$, we divide $v$ by its norm $‖v‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector With Respect to a Given Inner Product
canonical_examples.problem:
An inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  2x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + 3x_3 y_3.$ 
Calculate the norm of the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14057327/assets/1e710ca7b3b7bea626de36181a30869b0f114a4497843c6b6ea8b8966a91d208.png) under this inner product.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $\mathbf v$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\|\mathbf{v}\|$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{2\cdot (3\cdot 3)+2\cdot 2+3\cdot (1\cdot 1)} \\  & =\sqrt{18+4+3} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Polynomials
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V=\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ be the vector space of all polynomials of degree at most $2,$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle {x}(t), {y}(t) \rangle = x(1)y(1) + x(2)y(2) + x(3)y(3).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector  $p(t) = 1 - t^2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${p}(t) = 1-t^2,$ we obtain

$$
p(1)=0,\qquad 
p(2)= -3,\qquad 
p(3)=-8.
$$

Computing $\|p(t)\|$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(1)p(1)+p(2)p(2)+p(3)p(3)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}+[p(3)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+9+64} \\  & =\sqrt{73}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,1\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,1\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)= 2t-1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle  f(t),  f(t) \rangle}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}-2{t}^{2}+t)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-2+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Normalizing a Vector in an Inner Product Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $V=\mathcal{C}\left[0,\pi\right]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $\left[0,\pi\right],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
\langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

Normalize the vector $f(t)= 3t.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\| f(t)\| = \sqrt{\langle  f(t),  f(t) \rangle}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3t)}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }9{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =3{\pi }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\| f(t) \|  = \sqrt{3\pi^3} = \pi \sqrt{3\pi}.
$$

To normalize the vector $f(t),$ we divide $f(t)$ by its norm $\| f(t) \| \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\frac{f(t)}{‖f(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{3\pi }}\cdot 3t \\  & =\frac{t\sqrt{3}}{\pi \sqrt{\pi }}\end{aligned}
$$
